cues.text: In May 1656, a devastating outbreak of plague, likely carried by Spanish troops arriving from Sardinia, swept through the Kingdom of Naples in southern Italy, killing between half and sixty percent of the population in the hardest-hit areas.
The disease spread rapidly from Naples into the surrounding countryside and villages, eventually reaching the town of Cava dei Tirreni, where it cut the local population roughly in half.
Among the few clergy in Cava who survived the epidemic untouched was the parish priest, Father Paolo Franco.

Rather than retreat further into isolation as the contagion continued to spread, Franco felt called, despite the very real danger of infection, to lead the surviving townspeople in an act of public reparation.
On May 25, 1656, the feast of the Ascension, Franco organized a procession of the Blessed Sacrament.
It traveled from the district of the Santissima Annunziata to nearby Monte Castello’s summit, a fortified height overlooking the town and valley below.
The procession gathered the community for the climb despite the risk that close proximity posed during an active plague.
Reaching the terrace at the top of Monte Castello, Father Franco raised the Blessed Sacrament and blessed the town of Cava dei Tirreni spread out below.

According to the tradition kept in Cava ever since, the plague ceased in the town from that point forward, sparing the community further loss after the epidemic had already claimed thousands of lives in the surrounding region.

Cava dei Tirreni has marked the anniversary every year since 1657 with the Festa di Montecastello, a historical procession and reenactment now numbering among the longest-running traditions of its kind in Italy, drawing large crowds each June.

In April 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the town's clergy repeated the same blessing from the same summit, invoking the memory of 1656 in the hope of a similar deliverance from a new contagion nearly four centuries later.
